body: Take the Ind AS 24 related-party note each year, map each transaction to its expense line, and compute RPT / line. Flag a rising share or a near-monopoly (>50% of a line). VMM: the PE promoter vehicle Samayat Services LLP is also its transporter and warehouse operator (DRHP risk factor 16). Transport paid to Samayat: Rs 14.3 cr FY22 (13.8% of transport) -> Rs 25.6 cr FY24 (16.2%) -> Rs 72.1 cr FY26 (28.1% of Rs 256 cr). Warehousing: Rs 31.2 cr FY26 (47% of rent and warehousing, down from 62% in FY22). Rishay/Rishanth LLPs add admin and QC fees (~Rs 7 cr). About Rs 103 cr a year (~8% of pre-Ind AS EBITDA) goes to the controlling shareholder's entities. This is a soft flag, not a hard disqualifier (no sign of diversion; audit-committee approved). Open questions: rates vs third parties, contract fate when the PE stake falls, and the entity's MCA filings. Always ask what happens to RPT contracts at a sponsor exit.
title: Related-party share of each cost line, by year: the governance check no screen shows

body: Ben-David, Graham and Harvey, 'Managerial Miscalibration' (Quarterly Journal of Economics 128(4), 2013; ~745 Crossref citations): the Duke CFO Survey, more than 13,300 probability distributions for one-year S&P 500 returns given by US CFOs over 10 years (2001-2011). Realised returns fell inside the executives' own 80% confidence intervals only 36% of the time, so their intervals were far too narrow. They widened the lower bound in times of high uncertainty, but miscalibration was worst in exactly those periods. Executives who were miscalibrated about the market were similarly miscalibrated about their own firm's prospects, and firms with miscalibrated CFOs invested more and used more debt. Replicated: overprecision is the most robust overconfidence form in psychology (Moore-Healy 2008; Alpert-Raiffa 1982: '98% intervals' miss 40%+ of the time). Use for us: (1) management guidance ranges in Indian concalls ('15-20% growth', 'margins 18-20%') are probably far too narrow; the base-rate width is much wider, so haircut and widen; (2) our own valuation ranges and scenario bands are equally likely to be too narrow, so set 80% bands and then test how often outcomes land inside them; (3) aggressive capex plus debt alongside very confident guidance is the miscalibration combination that ends badly in cyclicals.
title: Executives are miscalibrated: CFOs' 80% intervals contained the realised market return only 36% of the time (Ben-David-Graham-Harvey 2013)
